blocks.title: pH curve and equivalence point
blocks.text: A pH curve (titration curve) is a graph of the pH of the solution against the volume of titrant added. The equivalence point is the point at which the amount of titrant added is just enough to neutralise the analyte solution completely. The end point of the titration occurs when the indicator changes colour; an indicator is chosen whose end point is close to the equivalence point.
Titration curves show how the pH of an acidic or basic solution changes as a basic or acidic solution is added, and they are used to choose an indicator that shows when the titration is complete.

Consider the titration of HCl with NaOH. Initially the solution contains only the strong acid, which dissociates completely, so [H+] is high and the pH very low. As NaOH is added, OH- ions neutralise the H+ ions of HCl and the pH rises. The equivalence point is reached when the amount of OH- added is stoichiometrically equal to the amount of H+ originally present; the pH at the equivalence point is 7.0. The curve here shows a steep rise, changing quickly from acidic to neutral, the pH at the end point changing from about 4.0 to 10.0. Since these titrations have pH 7.0 at equivalence, phenolphthalein can be used as indicator, as it shows different colours in this range.

blocks.alt: Titration curve: pH (0 to 14) against volume of strong base added (0 to 80 mL), with plotted points. The pH starts near 1, rises slowly, jumps almost vertically at 40 mL and levels off near 12.5. A dashed line marks pH = 7.00 at equivalence point. Coloured bands on the steep part show phenolphthalein (about pH 8.2 to 10) and methyl red (about pH 4.4 to 6.2), each labelled beside a flask.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.3: Strong acid-strong base titration curve (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.3).

blocks.text: Consider the titration of aqueous NH3 with HCl. Initially the solution contains only the weak base, which partially dissociates, giving a lower OH- concentration than a strong base; the initial pH is greater than 7 but lower than that of a strong base. As HCl is added the OH- concentration decreases and the pH falls. Before the equivalence point the solution is in a buffer-like region where the pH changes more gradually: the weak base and its conjugate acid (from the salt formed) create a buffering effect that moderates the pH change. The pH at the equivalence point is less than 7 (pH = 5.27) because the conjugate acid slightly dissociates, NH4+ giving NH3 + H+, making the solution acidic. After the equivalence point the pH falls rapidly, because the strong acid dissociates completely and supplies a high concentration of H+. Methyl orange changes colour in this range, so it serves as indicator for strong acid-weak base titrations.

blocks.alt: Titration curve: pH (0 to 14) against volume of HCl(aq) added (0 to 80 mL). The pH starts near 11, falls slowly through a buffer region (a pink band along the curve, also the phenolphthalein range), drops steeply at 40 mL and levels off near 1.5. Dashed lines mark about pH 9.2 and pH = 5.27 at equivalence point. A methyl red band crosses the steep drop, labelled beside a flask.
